---
title: "Is a winter nursery worth it?"
---

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4, dpi = 110)
```

A winter nursery, such as one in Puerto Rico for a US soybean program, adds a
second generation each year. A greenhouse can add a third. Lines reach the
yield trials sooner, so each breeding cycle takes fewer years. Each
off-season generation costs money, though: shipping, fees, labor and
greenhouse space. Is the speed worth the cost?

This article measures what the extra generations buy, then puts a price on
it.

```{r setup, message = FALSE}
library(tidyagsim)
library(ggplot2)
theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 12))
```

## Three speeds

We run the same pipeline for three cycles with one, two or three nursery
generations a year, and record every year as it goes:

```{r}
pipeline <- line_pipeline(
  generations_per_year = tune(),
  n_crosses = 30, progeny_per_cross = 15, n_ayt = 80, n_parents = 20, cycles = 3,
  founders = asr_founders(n_chr = 10, seg_sites = 100)
)

res <- tune_grid(
  pipeline,
  resamples = sim_replicates(12, seed = 1),
  grid = data.frame(generations_per_year = 1:3),
  metrics = sim_metric_set(release_gain, gain_per_year, years),
  control = control_sim(save_outcomes = TRUE)
)
collect_metrics(res, type = "wide")[, c("generations_per_year", "release_gain", "release_gain_se",
                                        "years", "gain_per_year")]
```

Look at `release_gain`: it is *identical* for the three speeds. In this
pipeline the nursery changes when things happen, not what happens. The same
crosses, the same lines and the same selections occur, just sooner. Because
every design runs on the same seeds, the simulation shows this exactly rather
than burying it in noise. What changes is time, and so gain per year:

```{r, fig.alt = "Mean genetic value of the parents against year for one, two and three generations per year. The same gains arrive sooner with more generations per year."}
traj <- collect_trajectories(res)
avg <- aggregate(mean ~ generations_per_year + year, data = traj, FUN = mean)
avg <- rbind(data.frame(generations_per_year = 1:3, year = 0, mean = 0), avg)
avg$speed <- factor(avg$generations_per_year, labels = c("Summer only", "+ winter nursery", "+ greenhouse"))

ggplot(avg, aes(year, mean, colour = speed)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) + geom_point() +
  labs(x = "Year", y = "Mean genetic value of parents (founder SDs)", colour = NULL,
       title = "The same gains, delivered sooner")
```

## What a year costs

Each cycle makes `r 30 * 15` lines, and every off-season generation is grown
for each of them. With F5-derived lines, two generations a year puts 2 of
the 5 nursery generations in the off-season and three a year puts 3 there.
Here is the extra cost per cycle, and per year saved, for three prices per
line per off-season generation:

```{r}
lines_per_cycle <- 30 * 15
speeds <- data.frame(option = c("+ winter nursery", "+ greenhouse"), generations_per_year = 2:3)
speeds$offseason_generations <- 5 - ceiling(5 / speeds$generations_per_year)
speeds$years_saved_per_cycle <- 5 / 1 - 5 / speeds$generations_per_year

costs <- merge(speeds, data.frame(price = c(2, 6, 12)))
costs$extra_cost_per_cycle <- costs$offseason_generations * lines_per_cycle * costs$price
costs$cost_per_year_saved <- costs$extra_cost_per_cycle / costs$years_saved_per_cycle
costs[order(costs$option, costs$price), ]
```

`line_pipeline()` does this accounting itself when you set
`offseason_cost`, and adds it to `cost`.

## Making the call

The simulation has turned the question into a single number for each option:
dollars per year saved. Whether that is worth paying depends on what a year
is worth to your program. That could be the value of releasing a variety a
year earlier, of responding sooner to a new disease, or of the extra cycles
completed over a career. The simulation cannot decide that for you, but it
makes the trade explicit.

```{r, fig.alt = "Cost per year saved against price per line per off-season generation for the winter nursery and greenhouse options."}
ggplot(costs, aes(price, cost_per_year_saved, colour = option)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) + geom_point(size = 2) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = function(x) paste0("$", format(x, big.mark = ","))) +
  labs(x = "Price per line per off-season generation ($)", y = "Cost per year saved (per cycle)",
       colour = NULL, title = "The price of speed")
```

## When the nursery changes more than timing

Here the nursery only moved events earlier, so its value is all about time.
Simulation earns its keep when speed also changes the genetics. Two examples:

* **More cycles in a fixed horizon.** Set `cycles` so each option fills the
  same number of years. Faster programs then complete more cycles, and the
  gains compound.
* **Overlapping cycles.** Real programs start new crosses every year and
  recycle parents from earlier trials. `line_pipeline()` runs cycles one
  after another. To model overlapping cycles, write the program with
  `alphasim_program()` and compare it with this one in a `sim_set()`.
